text:
“If we didn’t celebrate a goal, especially in this game, that would be madness,” Kike Salas said. Instead, this was madness, the kind of moment a derby is meant to have, even if it has nothing else. It was late, it was lucky, and there wasn’t even a winner but right there, right then, at 24 minutes past 8pm on Saturday evening in the Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán Stadium, it felt like there was. Frankly it was a bit rubbish, as bad a goal as you’ll see, but it was also the best, practically Pelé against the Nazis. Suddenly there were arms and legs everywhere, tears too. Cameras confirmed it. Zoom in and there they are: actual, real life tears.
In the 91st minute of the 146th meeting between Sevilla Fútbol Club and Real Betis Balompié – “derby of derbies” according to Luis García, the Sevilla coach for whom it was the first – Salas’s shot from 18 yards went through Marc Bartra’s legs and Álvaro Valles’s hands. The ball dribbled into the Betis net so apologetically it barely touched the net at all and hadn’t got there before Sevilla’s vice-captain was gone. Raised in Morón de la Frontera, to the south of a city divided, Salas joined Sevilla at 11; now, having levelled the game at 1-1, he went tearing towards the terraces, absolutely losing it like they were.
In the six-yard box, Robbie Ure, the Scottish striker who had watched the ball pass and whose own shot barely 100 seconds before was the eighth Betis blocked, resigned to the fact that it just wasn’t going to happen, reacted to the fact that it actually had with his right arm pumping like Animal on the drums. Screaming as he went, Salas thumped at his chest as hard. Around the Sánchez Pizjuán, 42,983 went wild except the 600 Béticos high in the corner. They couldn’t believe this and nor could their players: of all the ways to let go. From the Sevilla bench, everyone ran towards the team.
García went the other way through the crowd in his blue suit, like the final scene of a romcom: a man fighting against the rush-hour tide, bundling into a busy subway station desperate to reach the train before it leaves with her on board. He was in the middle of the pitch when he put the brakes on and returned, alone. He had been through the emotions; frustration, relief, joy, vindication and frustration again. A colleague awaited with a high five that was hard too. They could have won. But they also could have lost – Sevilla had trailed to Antony’s goal, which wasn’t great either, and Odysseas Vlachodimos’s superb save had prevented the Brazilian from getting Betis’s second and ending it – but at least they had salvaged a point.
At the final whistle, the Betis midfielder Dani Ceballos came to console Valles. “You’ve been our best player this season,” he told the goalkeeper, which was true. No one in La Liga has made more saves and none have been more significant either. Valles’s xG avoided is 8.3; the next best is 4.1. At the same time, Salas tried to do the post-game interview but couldn’t hear over the noise. Behind him, his family were waiting for a hug. As Betis’s players made their way, Sevilla’s players stood before supporters at the north end, applauding and applauded back.
“When you go to your greatest rivals’ ground, you deserve to win but they get a draw and on top of that they celebrate it, you know you’re doing things right,” said the Betis captain Bartra, who also claimed that Salas shouldn’t have been on the pitch to score the equaliser after he had trodden on Isco’s ankle. “A bad game from us only allows them to draw at home,” said the Betis president, Ángel Haro. “Fortunately, we’re in a period when a draw feels like sadness to us and a triumph for them.”
And so the debate was served, so the accusations came, the usual nonsense. In Spain? In Seville? Surely not?! Etc and so on. But if the words of Betis’s captain and president prompted that, if those words were a little pointed in a city where they pride themselves on being wind-up merchants and the derby is the most passionate in the country, there is an obvious response: well, yeah. Not least precisely because it’s about putting one over on each other. Every goal is an explosion and Sevilla got theirs in the 91st minute. Against Betis. From the centre-back who’s been at the club half his life. Of course they celebrated it.
If it might have seemed a little odd for Sevilla to stand there before their fans celebrating when they hadn’t won and a run of one win in seven in the league had been confirmed, that too was part of it. Because Bartra and Haro were right, to their credit and to Sevilla’s too. At the start of this derby, a huge banner came down over the north stand; a supporters’ work of art made by hand as ever, it lauded a history of greatness, but maybe history is the word, and that’s the real greatness: it is three years since Sevilla won a trophy or qualified for Europe, those days not just fading fast but long gone, yet here they are anyway, more than 35,000 of them every week.
Sevilla are a club in crisis, where the former president José María del Nido is at war with the former president José María del Nido – and, yes, they are father and son. Where the debt is almost €200m (£167.2m) and the solution, a sale to a consortium led by Sergio Ramos, fell through. Where they have the lowest salary limit in the whole of primera, at €20m (£16.7m), and four second division teams were allowed to spend more. Where this summer they had a net spend of minus €25m (£20.9m). And where they qualified for the Champions League three years running under Julen Lopetegui, sacked him, went through seven managers in three years and finished 12th, 14th and 17th, closer to relegation every season.
In May they finished 13th yet only escaped relegation in the penultimate week, and that was a miracle. The day that García had been presented as coach, arriving on a rescue mission that seemed impossible, the sporting director was overheard saying: “It’s like a funeral in here”.
Meanwhile, Betis have been heading in the other direction. Sevilla’s first division league positions since 2006 read: 5, 3, 5, 3, 3, 4, 5, 9, 9, 5, 5, 7, 4, 7, 6, 4, 4, 4, then: 12, 14, 17, 13. Betis’s read: 14, 16, 13, 18 and relegation … then, after two years away, 13, 7, 20 and relegation again, followed by 10, 15, 6, 10, 15. And then, under Manuel Pellegrini: 6, 5, 6, 7, 6, 5. While Sevilla crumbled, Betis consolidated. Under the Chilean they have won a Copa del Rey – one of only three in their history – and this season are back in the Champions League, 20 years on. Defeated just twice, they sit fourth. Their salary limit is seven times Sevilla’s.
The only thing missing, some said, was precisely this: the derby. “I think I’ve always understood the importance for our people,” Pellegrini said, “but if you ask me, I would prefer to finisher higher up than to win the derby.” From 2020-2025 Betis won only one of 10 – although that was in the cup en route to winning it. Then they beat Sevilla 2-1 in March 2025, and again in December; they came into Saturday night without defeat in three, an inescapable superiority imposed. At the end on Saturday night, Antony turned to the Sevilla fans and mouthed: “You’re very bad, you’re terrible.”
It was born of anger but not entirely untrue. These may be the best days of Betis’s lives, possibly even ever. For Sevilla, it’s different, the limitations clear. Yet García has got more from them: the team seemingly destined to fight for their lives again went into this game in a European place. And while it is worth a word of warning here – after four victories in their first six, Sevilla are on a miserable run, reality creeping back in – they came out having competed again, a team. Bad they might be, but Antony and his teammates hadn’t been able to beat them. Only Atlético, Real Madrid, Barcelona and Getafe have.
In fact, Sevilla hadn’t just competed. When Pellegrini described this as the “typical derby” where neither side did much, García suggested he must have been watching a different match, insisting that the draw was bittersweet because his players had deserved more. Still, at least it wasn’t just bitter. When Salas scored and sent everyone wild, it was their 25th shot, something like justice done and something like satisfaction found, something to hold on to and why not? Not least because as well as against their rivals it had been done, the coach said, against a great team: a Champions League side full of talent. In this city of symbiosis, these years of change, Betis’s success was indeed the measure of Sevilla’s and vice versa, just as it always was. And the way it came, tension liberated late in the night that means more to them than any other, was reason to celebrate. That’s what football is for. Anything other than madness then would have been madness.
